content:
Offloading keyboard shortcuts to a programmable macro keyboard is the best productivity trick I've ever done.

The keyboard shortcut exploration journey

My initial foray into keyboard shortcuts started with simple macOS triggers, like using @@ to enter my primary email address, and similar shortcuts for my full name, address, phone number, zip code, and more.

Then I decided to level up, using Keyboard Maestro to set up keyboard shortcuts to open some of my most-used folders and apps.

From the desktop to the downloads folder to work-related folders, hitting Fn+F1 through Fn+F6 became pure muscle memory, taking me places that previously required multiple clicks. Other function keys are dedicated to opening favorite apps and sites, plus Keyboard Maestro's clipboard history switcher.

I then started automating parts of my workflow further, including opening QuickTime and starting a new recording, as well as automatically opening Shure PlusMOTI when a specific USB-C microphone is plugged in.

Not long after, I also custom-set shortcuts for Adobe Audition's tools, settings, and panel configurations — some of which I quickly moved to the Logitech MX Master mouse for even faster editing.

Leveling up further

This setup worked for me for a long time, until one day, my 9to5Mac colleague Gui Rambo introduced me to a small 12-key plus 3-knob macro keyboard he had purchased. I was immediately intrigued, and followed suit.

Once it arrived, I quickly discovered that some additional setup was required to make it work properly with macOS. Luckily, a GitHub project handled all the heavy lifting, and ChatGPT helped me complete the rest.

One of the great things about this setup is that having a dedicated keyboard for triggering Keyboard Maestro shortcuts means I don't have to memorize them or worry about ergonomics.

What's more, because this keyboard can offer up to 3 layers of 12 key shortcuts, and the knobs can also be pressed as buttons, I can have one mode of operation while using Adobe Audition, and an entirely different mode while operating the system.

When using Adobe Audition, this macro keyboard combined with the MX Master mouse lets me switch between tools, export files (or just specific selections), apply effects like normalization, compression, dereverb, dehiss, ripple delete, and more — orders of magnitude faster than using regular keyboard shortcuts, let alone no shortcuts at all, and with much smoother workflow.

In the operating system, I can switch the same keyboard to another layer and just as easily change audio input, adjust volume, tweak screen brightness, mute or unmute the microphone, and open frequently used folders.

Admittedly, it took me a while to memorize all these commands, but it became second nature much faster than expected. More importantly, when I have to work in an environment without this setup, honestly, the Mac feels broken to me.

Plus, macro keyboards come in countless configurations and options — shapes, sizes, keys, knobs, light colors, you name it. It's a truly seemingly endless field of exploration. If your work involves any repetitive operations (and whose doesn't?), I wholeheartedly recommend diving in yourself.
